difficultyReason: The argument contains an intermediate conclusion, an embedded concession, and a final inference. Students must track three logical moves to identify the correct abstract description. Trap choices describe partial moves or reverse the direction of inference.
stimulus: Physician: Some of my colleagues argue that a patient who has not responded to two successive antidepressant medications should automatically be considered treatment-resistant and switched to electroconvulsive therapy. I agree that non-response to two medications is a reliable indicator of treatment resistance in most patients. Nevertheless, there is a well-documented subgroup of patients who fail to respond to those medications solely because of undetected drug interactions caused by concurrent prescriptions. For such patients, treatment resistance is not the correct diagnosis. Therefore, automatic reclassification after two failed medications is unwarranted without first ruling out pharmacological interference.

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting a general principle endorsed by an opposing view, then identifying a class of exceptions that prevents applying that principle universally

choices.label: B
choices.text: providing a counterexample to a statistical generalization and concluding that the generalization should be abandoned entirely

choices.label: C
choices.text: deriving an absurd consequence from a rival position in order to establish that the rival position is self-contradictory

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring a causal relationship between drug interactions and treatment resistance from the correlation observed in a large clinical sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing the authority of clinical colleagues to support the claim that electroconvulsive therapy is the preferred second-line treatment

explanations.correct: The physician explicitly grants that non-response to two medications is a reliable indicator of treatment resistance — the general principle colleagues rely on — then carves out an exception subgroup (drug-interaction patients) to argue the principle cannot be applied automatically. This is precisely 'accepting the general principle but identifying exceptions that limit its universal application.'
explanations.B: Partially true trap: the physician does identify an exception subgroup, but does not argue that the generalization should be abandoned entirely — the physician explicitly endorses the generalization as reliable in most cases.
explanations.C: No absurd consequence is derived; the physician never claims the colleagues' position is internally contradictory.
explanations.D: No clinical sample or correlation is cited; the drug-interaction subgroup is introduced as a documented category, not as the product of a new causal inference.
explanations.E: The physician disagrees with colleagues rather than appealing to their authority, and nowhere endorses ECT as the preferred treatment.

difficultyReason: The argument uses an analogy between two domains (economics and ecology) as an intermediate step before reaching a policy conclusion. Answer choices differ in subtle ways — one correctly identifies the two-domain analogy while others misdescribe the direction of inference or the type of reasoning.
stimulus: Economist: When a dominant firm in a market suddenly exits, smaller competitors rarely fill the void immediately; instead, productivity in the sector declines for years before recovery. Ecologists have documented a structurally identical pattern: when a keystone predator is removed from an ecosystem, subordinate species do not simply expand to occupy the vacated niche, and overall biodiversity declines sharply before a new equilibrium emerges. Given this parallel, economic policymakers who are considering breaking up a dominant technology firm should expect a prolonged period of reduced innovation, not the immediate competitive flourishing that proponents of the breakup predict.
questionStem: The economist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizing from a large number of economic cases to predict the outcome of a specific proposed policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between a well-documented pattern in ecology and a structurally similar situation in economics to support a prediction about policy outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to an established economic principle to argue that a proposed action will have the opposite of its intended effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: using historical data about past regulatory interventions to predict that a proposed breakup will reduce innovation

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting the proponents' prediction by showing that it relies on a definition of competition that is too narrow

explanations.correct: The economist introduces ecological evidence about keystone predators, explicitly identifies it as structurally parallel to the economic situation, and uses that cross-domain analogy to forecast prolonged reduced innovation. Choice B captures this two-domain analogical inference precisely.
explanations.A: Partially true trap: the economist does cite economic cases, but the core logical move is the cross-domain analogy to ecology, not a generalization from many economic cases alone.
explanations.C: No established economic principle is invoked by name; the argument works through analogy, not a named principle. The 'opposite effect' language fits, but the mechanism described is wrong.
explanations.D: The evidence comes from ecology, not from historical data about past regulatory interventions — this is an accurate-sounding but content-displaced description.
explanations.E: No definitional dispute about 'competition' appears anywhere in the argument.

difficultyReason: The argument eliminates alternatives to reach a conclusion by elimination, but also contains a concession. Students must distinguish the eliminative structure from the partially true trap describing it as a generalization from examples.
stimulus: Historian: The rapid abandonment of the gold standard by industrialized nations in the 1930s is sometimes attributed to ideological shifts among economists, and sometimes to coordinated international political pressure. But detailed archival research has shown that economists of the era were deeply divided rather than ideologically unified, and that the relevant international negotiations had collapsed well before the abandonments occurred. The only remaining explanation that is consistent with the archival record is that individual governments abandoned the gold standard in direct response to domestic unemployment crises that made currency deflation politically untenable.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing expert consensus among economic historians to establish that domestic unemployment was the decisive factor in abandoning the gold standard

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the political pressures of the 1930s and those of a more recent economic crisis to support the preferred explanation

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating competing explanations on the basis of archival evidence and inferring that the remaining explanation is correct

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from several specific national cases to conclude that domestic unemployment universally drives currency policy changes

choices.label: E
choices.text: accepting one of the two competing explanations as partially correct and incorporating it into a revised account

explanations.correct: The historian names two rival explanations, uses archival evidence to show each is inconsistent with the historical record, and then infers that the only remaining explanation must be correct. This is argument by elimination.
explanations.A: No expert consensus is cited; the historian actively notes that economists were divided, which is the opposite of consensus.
explanations.B: No analogy to a more recent crisis appears anywhere in the stimulus.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap: the historian infers a specific historical explanation, not a universal generalization about all currency policy changes.
explanations.E: The historian dismisses both competing explanations rather than accepting either as partially correct.

difficultyReason: The argument applies an abstract legal principle to a concrete case, but the principle is stated in conditional form and the application involves a non-obvious intermediate step. Trap choices misidentify the direction of the inference or describe the argument as an analogy rather than a principle application.
stimulus: Legal scholar: A contract is enforceable only if the party against whom enforcement is sought had a genuine opportunity to read and understand its terms before agreeing. Software end-user license agreements are typically presented in small print after payment has been made and the product has been downloaded. At that point, the user has no practical alternative to clicking 'agree,' because declining would require returning a product the user has already used. Accordingly, software license agreements of this type do not satisfy the condition for enforceability and should not be treated as binding contracts.
questionStem: The legal scholar's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses an analogy between software license agreements and other adhesion contracts to argue that both should be treated as unenforceable

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general principle governing contract enforceability to a specific category of agreements and derives a conclusion about their legal status

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between the timing of disclosure and consumer harm from survey data about user comprehension

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejects a rival legal standard by deriving a consequence from it that contradicts a widely accepted judicial precedent

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishes that software companies act in bad faith by demonstrating that license agreements are designed to prevent meaningful consent

explanations.correct: The scholar states a general principle (enforceability requires genuine opportunity to read and understand terms), argues that software EULAs as described fail to meet that condition, and concludes they are unenforceable. This is a straightforward principle-application-to-case structure.
explanations.A: No other category of adhesion contracts is mentioned; the argument works by applying a principle, not by drawing an analogy to a sister category.
explanations.C: No survey data or causal inference appears; the argument is purely a principled deduction.
explanations.D: No rival legal standard is named and no judicial precedent is cited; the scholar offers a direct principled argument.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap: the scholar nowhere attributes bad faith or intent to software companies; the argument is about structural features of the agreement, not corporate motive.

difficultyReason: The argument cites a single verifiable counterexample to defeat a universal claim, but the counterexample is embedded in a longer setup that could mislead students into thinking the main move is a causal inference or a generalization. The partially-true trap accurately describes a secondary move.
stimulus: Linguist: Proponents of the critical-period hypothesis claim that any individual who does not acquire a first language before puberty will be permanently incapable of achieving full grammatical competence in any language. However, documented cases of late-language-acquisition individuals — such as those raised in extreme social isolation — show that some adults who had no language exposure before puberty do eventually acquire the grammar of a taught language to a level indistinguishable from that of native speakers, at least in controlled testing environments. This demonstrates that the critical-period hypothesis, in its strongest universal form, is false.

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizing from documented cases of late language acquisition to conclude that critical periods do not exist for any aspect of language development

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a principle about developmental windows in biology to argue that the critical-period hypothesis overstates the evidence

choices.label: C
choices.text: identifying a verifiable instance that contradicts a universal claim and concluding that the claim in its strongest form cannot be sustained

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from a correlation between social isolation and language delay that puberty itself is not the cause of permanent grammatical deficits

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that the critical-period hypothesis applies in most cases while arguing that its proponents have misidentified the relevant developmental mechanism

explanations.correct: The linguist explicitly targets the 'strongest universal form' of the hypothesis ('any individual… will be permanently incapable') and cites documented cases of late acquirers who achieved native-level competence. One genuine counterexample is logically sufficient to refute a universal claim, and that is exactly the move being made.
explanations.A: Mis-scaled trap: the linguist's conclusion is specifically about the universal form of the hypothesis, not a sweeping generalization that critical periods don't exist for any aspect of language at all.
explanations.B: No biological developmental-window principle is invoked; the argument stays within linguistics and uses a direct counterexample.
explanations.D: The argument does not pursue a causal analysis of puberty vs. social isolation as competing causal factors; it uses the cases as counterexamples, not as evidence for an alternative causal chain.
explanations.E: The linguist does not concede the hypothesis applies in most cases — the conclusion is that the universal form is false, not that it is mechanistically misdescribed.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a reductio structure: it conditionally accepts a rival claim and shows it entails an empirically false consequence. Distinguishing a reductio from a direct counterexample is challenging; the partial-truth trap names the consequence without identifying the conditional structure.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: Proponents of large-scale iron fertilization of the oceans argue that seeding the surface ocean with iron will cause phytoplankton blooms large enough to sequester atmospheric carbon at a scale sufficient to meaningfully offset industrial emissions. If this were true, we would expect to observe sustained high-carbon organic matter sinking to deep-sea sediments in proportion to the bloom size in every large-scale fertilization trial conducted to date. Yet in every such trial, the expected carbon export to deep sediments has been negligible relative to the bloom size, with most carbon recycled in the surface layer. The proposed mechanism therefore does not operate as proponents describe.
questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: argues that the rival claim, if true, would require an outcome that empirical trials have consistently failed to produce, and concludes that the claim is incorrect

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites a single anomalous trial result to cast doubt on the generalization that iron fertilization sequesters carbon

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws an analogy between deep-sea carbon cycling and terrestrial carbon storage to challenge the proposed sequestration mechanism

choices.label: D
choices.text: accepts the proponents' goal of carbon sequestration while rejecting their proposed method on grounds of economic inefficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers from the correlation between bloom size and surface-layer recycling that iron fertilization causes net increases in atmospheric carbon

explanations.correct: The scientist conditionally assumes the proponents' claim ('if this were true'), derives what would have to be observable (deep-sediment carbon export proportional to bloom size), notes that every trial fails to show this, and concludes the proposed mechanism is wrong. This is a conditional-derivation / reductio-style refutation.
explanations.B: Partially true trap: multiple trials are cited, not a single anomalous result; and the argument's structure is a reductio, not merely a counterexample citation.
explanations.C: No analogy to terrestrial carbon storage appears; the argument relies on trial data within oceanography alone.
explanations.D: Economic inefficiency is never mentioned; the argument is about whether the mechanism works as described, not about cost.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap with content distortion: the scientist does not infer that iron fertilization increases atmospheric carbon — the conclusion is only that the sequestration mechanism doesn't operate as claimed.

difficultyReason: The argument first establishes an intermediate conclusion via a causal claim, then uses that intermediate conclusion as a premise in a further ethical inference. Students must recognize the two-step structure — empirical premise to intermediate conclusion, then intermediate conclusion to normative conclusion — and not select a choice that describes only the first or only the second step.
stimulus: Ethicist: Architects who design buildings without adequate accessibility features are often said to be merely complying with client budgetary constraints. But the unavailability of physical access demonstrably excludes people with disabilities from civic participation — from voting locations, courtrooms, and public offices — that is legally guaranteed to them. Any professional practice that predictably produces outcomes in which legally guaranteed rights are systematically denied constitutes a form of complicity in rights violations. Therefore, architects who knowingly design inaccessible public buildings bear a form of professional moral responsibility for the exclusions that result.

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between architectural decisions and legal decisions to argue that architects should be held to the same accountability standards as judges

choices.label: B
choices.text: first establishing empirically that inaccessible design produces rights-excluding outcomes, then applying a moral principle to those outcomes to derive a conclusion about professional responsibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizing from a series of individual architects' decisions to conclude that the profession as a whole endorses discriminatory design practices

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting the budget-constraint defense by demonstrating that it is internally inconsistent with professional codes of ethics

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring that architects intend to exclude people with disabilities from the fact that they knowingly produce buildings that have that effect

explanations.correct: The ethicist first makes an empirical claim (inaccessible design excludes people with disabilities from legally guaranteed civic participation) and treats that as an established intermediate conclusion. The ethicist then invokes a moral principle (any practice that predictably produces rights violations is complicity) and applies it to derive the normative conclusion about architects' moral responsibility. Choice B captures this two-step empirical-then-normative structure.
explanations.A: No analogy between architects and judges is drawn; architects and courthouses appear, but courts are examples of excluded civic venues, not analogical comparators for architects' roles.
explanations.C: Mis-scaled trap: the conclusion is about individual architects who knowingly design inaccessibly, not a generalization about the profession's collective endorsement of discrimination.
explanations.D: The budget-constraint defense is acknowledged but not refuted by showing it is internally inconsistent; the ethicist simply bypasses it by grounding the conclusion in a separate principle.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap: the ethicist concludes responsibility, not intent. The argument explicitly works from predictable outcomes, not from inferred mental states.

difficultyReason: The argument uses an appeal to definition as its core move, but the definition is stipulated mid-argument after an empirical description, making the logical structure harder to identify. Traps include a partially-true causal inference and a misdescribed generalization.
stimulus: Technology critic: Supporters of algorithmic content curation claim that recommendation engines merely help users find content they would already prefer. But a preference, properly understood, is a disposition that exists prior to and independently of the choices presented to a person. When a recommendation engine systematically withholds entire categories of content from a user's feed, the user has no opportunity to form a preference regarding that content. What the algorithm produces, therefore, is not the satisfaction of pre-existing preferences but the creation of artificially constrained preference profiles — meaning that the claim that curation merely serves user preferences is false by definition.
questionStem: The technology critic's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical research showing that users exposed to algorithmically curated content report lower satisfaction than users who browse without algorithmic assistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: invoking a stipulated definition of 'preference' to show that what recommendation engines produce cannot qualify as the satisfaction of user preferences

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between algorithmic curation and traditional editorial decisions to argue that both manipulate audience preferences

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from the behavior of a few poorly designed recommendation engines to condemn all algorithmic curation

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring from the correlation between content withholding and narrowed user interests that algorithms cause long-term preference decay

explanations.correct: The critic defines 'preference' as a disposition formed prior to and independently of presented choices, then argues that because recommendation engines prevent users from encountering content, no genuine preference regarding that content can form — so the engine cannot be 'satisfying preferences' in the defined sense. The phrase 'false by definition' signals this explicitly.
explanations.A: No empirical user-satisfaction research is cited anywhere in the argument.
explanations.C: No analogy to traditional editorial decisions appears; the argument is entirely internal to the analysis of algorithmic curation.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap: the critic does not limit the argument to 'a few poorly designed' engines — the structural point is meant to apply to recommendation engines generally insofar as they withhold categories of content.
explanations.E: Causal inference trap: the conclusion is about whether curation satisfies preferences by definition, not about a long-term causal effect on preference formation.

difficultyReason: The argument establishes a conclusion about current policy by using evidence from a historical case as the direct basis for inference about an analogous present situation, but the analogical structure is obscured by the long historical setup and the embedded concession that the two situations differ in one respect. Students must identify which similarities drive the inference and whether the conceded difference defeats the analogy.
stimulus: Policy analyst: Critics of the proposed urban density mandate point out that a similar mandatory densification policy introduced in a major European city in the 1970s led to increased traffic congestion that persisted for over a decade. Admittedly, that city had a less developed public transit infrastructure than the city targeted by the current proposal. However, the mechanism behind the congestion — an influx of new residents whose daily travel patterns had not yet adapted to the density — operates independently of the quality of existing transit, as transit adoption takes years regardless of system quality. The critics' caution is therefore well founded: the proposed mandate is likely to produce the same kind of prolonged congestion.
questionStem: The policy analyst's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepts a disanalogy between a historical case and the current situation, argues that the disanalogy does not undermine the relevant parallel, and uses the historical case to support a prediction about the current policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: establishes a general causal law about urban densification and applies it to the current proposal to predict a specific negative outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismisses the critics' concern by showing that the historical case they rely on is not sufficiently similar to the current situation

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers from a series of historical densification failures that mandatory density mandates are always counterproductive

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses a comparison of transit infrastructure quality across cities to argue that the current city is better prepared for densification than the historical case

explanations.correct: The analyst acknowledges the critics' disanalogy (the historical city had worse transit), but neutralizes it by arguing the congestion-causing mechanism operates independently of transit quality. Having neutralized the disanalogy, the analyst uses the historical case as an analogy to predict the same prolonged congestion. This is a three-move structure: acknowledge disanalogy → neutralize it → deploy the analogy.
explanations.B: No general causal law is formally established across multiple cases; the analyst works from a single historical parallel, not a law derived from many instances.
explanations.C: Direction-reversal trap: the analyst does the opposite — supports the critics' concern rather than dismissing it, and preserves the similarity rather than undermining it.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap: the conclusion is about this specific proposal, not a universal generalization that all mandatory density mandates are always counterproductive.
explanations.E: Content-reversal trap: the analyst concedes the historical city had worse transit (less developed), then argues that doesn't matter — never claims the current city is better prepared.

difficultyReason: The argument combines a distinction between two senses of a term with an argument by elimination, then uses both moves together to reach a conclusion. Traps include answers describing only one of the two moves, and an extreme-verb answer falsely attributing a refutation of expert consensus.
stimulus: Art critic: When people say that a work of art is 'difficult,' they sometimes mean that it requires specialized training to appreciate, and sometimes mean that it resists full comprehension even for trained experts. These are entirely different claims. Works that merely require training are difficult only in the way that advanced mathematics is difficult: the difficulty is contingent on education and disappears with sufficient exposure. Works that resist expert comprehension, by contrast, are difficult in a deeper sense. The compositions of a certain late modernist composer have been extensively studied by trained musicians for decades, and professional analyses remain genuinely divergent and inconclusive. The composer's work is therefore not merely educationally difficult but irreducibly so.
questionStem: The art critic's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between musical difficulty and mathematical difficulty to conclude that both forms of difficulty are educationally contingent

choices.label: B
choices.text: surveying expert critical opinion on the composer's work to establish that the work has been misclassified by earlier critics

choices.label: C
choices.text: distinguishing two senses of a term, eliminating one sense as inapplicable, and concluding that the other sense correctly characterizes the case at hand

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from the divergence of expert analyses that the composer's work is of higher aesthetic quality than works that admit of consensus interpretation

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuting the consensus view among music scholars by demonstrating that their training is insufficient to resolve the work's fundamental ambiguities

explanations.correct: The critic opens by distinguishing two senses of 'difficult' (educationally contingent vs. irreducibly resistant to expert comprehension), then shows that the composer's work does not fit the first sense (since decades of expert study have not resolved it), and concludes it fits the second sense. The structure is: draw a distinction → eliminate one horn → apply the other.
explanations.A: Partially true trap: the analogy to mathematics is used to characterize the first sense of difficulty — the sense being eliminated — not to reach the conclusion. The math analogy is a subsidiary move, not the main technique.
explanations.B: No claim is made that earlier critics misclassified the work; the critic is drawing a distinction and applying it fresh, not correcting prior misclassification.
explanations.D: Extreme-verb trap with content distortion: the critic draws no conclusion about aesthetic quality or superiority; the argument is about the category of difficulty, not about evaluative ranking.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap: the critic does not refute a consensus view among scholars nor claim their training is insufficient. The divergence of expert opinion is cited as evidence that the difficulty is irreducible, not as a criticism of the experts.
